Q: CSS: Format of font-family A:

Q: Online MariaDB Server can't be accessed outside of MariaDB command Line A:

The error Access denied for user 'user'@'password' means your PHP code is passing the password where the host belongs. You can see the host part of the error is literally your password. The MariaDB CLI works because you're probably typing the flags in the right order there.

Just swap the arguments so they match what mysqli_connect expects:

$conn = mysqli_connect('hostname', 'user', 'your_actual_password', 'database');

I'd check your HeidiSQL settings too. It's likely the same issue where a field is swapped or misplaced. But the error string is the dead giveaway here.

Q: Could a class type with deleted default constructor be initialized using list initialization syntax Type t{}; A:

I think the standard just means "if T is a class type with deleted default constructor then goto default initialization". It would fail at last because the constructor selected for default initialization is deleted. It's used to distinguish with the 2nd case, i.e. "if T is a class type with a default constructor that is neither user-provided nor deleted", for that case zero-initialization is performed firstly, then default-initialization if T has a non-trivial default constructor.

A a{} is OK,but why?

Because when A is an aggregate type aggregate initialization is performed. Note that explicitly deleted constructors are allowed for aggregate type since C++11.

In all cases, if the empty pair of braces {} is used and T is an aggregate type, aggregate-initialization is performed instead of value-initialization.

And

An aggregate is one of the following types:

  • ...
  • class type (typically, struct or union), that has
    • ...
    • no user-provided, inherited, or explicit constructors (explicitly defaulted or deleted constructors are allowed) (since C++17) (until C++20)
    • ...

EDIT

Since C++20 the behavior changed; A a{}; would fail.

An aggregate is one of the following types:

  • ...
  • class type (typically, struct or union), that has
    • ...
    • no user-declared or inherited constructors (since C++20)
    • ...

A is not an aggregate again. A a{}; performs value-initialization (default-initialization), the deleted constructor is used and fails.

Q: Fix Rabbitmq connection timeout in springboot A:

Add in the application.properties:

spring.rabbitmq.connection-timeout=10000
spring.rabbitmq.host=localhost
spring.rabbitmq.port=9000
spring.rabbitmq.username=guest
spring.rabbitmq.password=guest

Q: Use the ADO OpenSchema Method to get table list, column list and value A:

Change your Code for Sub ListValues as Directed:

  Private Sub ListValues(ByVal db_file As String, ByVal db_table_name as String, ByVal        
  db_column_name As String)
  Dim statement As String
  Dim conn As ADODB.Connection
  Dim rs As ADODB.Recordset

' Open a connection

  Set conn = New ADODB.Connection
  conn.ConnectionString = _
  "Provider=Microsoft.Jet.OLEDB.4.0;" & _
  "Data Source=" & db_file & ";" & _
  "Persist Security Info=False"
  conn.Open

lstValues.Clear

Set rs = New ADODB.Recordset

rs.Open "SELECT*FROM " & db_table_name & " WHERE " & db_column_name, conn, adOpenStatic, adLockOptimistic

Do While Not rs.EOF
     lstValues.AddItem rs.Fields(db_column_name).Value
     rs.MoveNext
Loop

rs.Close
conn.Close
End Sub

Another Mistake in your coding:

Your Code:
    Set rs = conn.OpenSchema(adSchemaIndexes, _
    Array(Empty, Empty, Empty, Empty,db_column_name))

Right code:
    Set rs = conn.OpenSchema(adSchemaIndexes, _
    Array(Empty, Empty, Empty, Empty,db_table_name))

Q: pandas running notnull() sum() versus count() against the dataframe A:

df.notnull().sum() and df.notnull().count() do completely different things — that's why you get different results.

  • df.notnull().sum() — counts how many values are True (not null). So it gives you 3 for Name because only 3 rows have a real name.

  • df.notnull().count() — counts the total number of rows in the column, including NaN rows. It ignores whether the value is null or not. That's why you get 4 — because you have 4 rows total.

Think of it this way:

  • sum() → counts the True values only

  • count() → counts all rows

If you want to count non-null values only, always use notnull().sum() or just df.count() directly — which skips NaN by default:
df.count() # same as df.notnull().sum()
None in pandas is treated as NaN so it is correctly excluded from notnull().sum() but still counted by count() on the notnull boolean DataFrame.
